opus-5.5.text:
I think we have to be careful about drawing a general conclusion from one failed implementation. Synthetic data isn't a single thing you either "use" or "don't use." It's a whole pipeline, and the quality of that pipeline decides almost everything.

If someone renders some objects in a simulator, trains a policy, and it doesn't transfer to the real robot, the natural reaction is "synthetic data doesn't work." But when you look closely, the problem is usually somewhere specific. Maybe the physics wasn't accurate enough for that kind of contact. Maybe the visual domain gap was too large, so the lighting, materials and textures weren't randomized well. Maybe the object assets weren't diverse enough, or the task distribution in simulation didn't match what the robot actually sees. Or maybe the scale simply wasn't there. Each of these is an engineering and research problem you can work on. None of them is a fundamental proof that the approach is wrong.

In our own work, especially on grasping and dexterous manipulation, we spent years getting these details right: building large asset libraries, generating physically plausible grasps at the scale of billions, designing the randomization, and carefully closing the sim-to-real gap step by step. Our first versions didn't work well either. If we had stopped at the first failure, we would have concluded exactly what those people concluded. Once the pipeline became mature, though, the models trained purely on synthetic data could generalize zero-shot to novel objects in the real world, sometimes better than models trained on limited real data.

So my view is that a negative result from one implementation tells you about that implementation. It doesn't tell you about the ceiling of the method. Real data is extremely valuable, and I'm not saying we shouldn't collect it. But real data is expensive and slow to scale, and it's hard to cover the long tail. Synthetic data is one of the few ways I see to get the scale embodied intelligence needs. The right attitude is to ask *why* it failed and fix that, rather than dismiss the whole direction.

r001.rationale: The response says a failed implementation may reflect specific pipeline problems and cautions against concluding from that failure that synthetic data is ineffective overall.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most of those people are right about their own experiment and wrong about the conclusion. When someone says "synthetic data didn't work for us," what they usually mean is that they took an existing model, had it generate a pile of samples that looked like their training distribution, dumped it into the mix, and the eval either stayed flat or got worse. And that's a real result. I don't doubt it. But it's a bit like saying "we tried distributed training and it was slower," without asking whether the interconnect was the bottleneck.

The thing people underestimate is that synthetic data is not a single technique, it's a whole design space, and the easy corner of that space is almost worthless. If you generate data that the model could already produce, you're mostly teaching it its own habits back, and in the worst case you get the collapse effect where diversity shrinks with every round. So the "didn't work" cases I've looked at almost always share a few features: no verifier or filter in the loop, no attempt to target where the model is actually weak, and no measurement of whether the synthetic distribution covers anything the real data didn't.

The cases where it works look completely different. There's some external signal of correctness, whether that's a compiler, a unit test, a symbolic checker, or a stronger model acting as a judge with a clear rubric. The generation is steered toward the long tail, the stuff that's rare or expensive in natural data. And there's a lot of unglamorous engineering around deduplication, difficulty calibration, and mixing ratios. When I talk to teams that are getting real gains, maybe a quarter of their effort is the generation itself, and the rest is the filtering and the eval infrastructure. People who skipped that part and then declared the whole idea dead are, in a sense, reporting that the cheap version is cheap for a reason.

I'd also say there's a selection effect in who talks about it. The groups where it's working best have strong incentives not to publish the details, because the recipe is the moat. So the public conversation is skewed toward the negative anecdotes. That's not evidence the technique fails, it's evidence that the knowledge is concentrated.

So my attitude toward the skeptics is not to argue with their data point. I'd ask them what their filter was, what their eval looked like, and whether they were trying to fill a gap or just inflate token count. Usually the conversation ends somewhere more interesting than "it works" or "it doesn't."

r001.rationale: The response says people may be right that synthetic data failed in their experiment but wrong to generalize, and explains that weak implementations—such as unfiltered generation without targeting model weaknesses—can cause those failures.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish between “it didn’t work in my setup” and “synthetic data doesn’t work.” The first is a useful observation; the second is a much broader claim. You could have a problem with the data quality, the task you’re generating data for, or how you use it in training. A failed experiment doesn’t tell you which of those is responsible.

At the same time, we shouldn’t dismiss negative results. The useful question is: What did you try, and under what conditions did it fail? That helps us understand where synthetic data is useful and where it isn’t. It’s not automatically valuable just because you can generate a lot of it.

r001.rationale: The response says a failed experiment may stem from a problem in how someone uses synthetic data in training, so the failure could reflect their own implementation rather than synthetic data being ineffective generally.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between “it didn’t work in my setup” and “synthetic data doesn’t work.” The first is a useful observation; the second is a much broader claim. There are many reasons an implementation might fail: what you generate, how closely it matches the task, how you check its quality, and how you use it during training.

That doesn’t mean we should dismiss negative results. We should ask what failed and what the experiment actually tells us. Synthetic data isn’t automatically useful just because you can generate a lot of it. The question is whether it supplies something the model needs. If it doesn’t, making more of it may not help.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a failure in someone’s setup from a general claim that synthetic data does not work, and says implementation choices can cause failures.
